title: China Southwest Airlines 4509
summary: Flight 4509, a Tupolev Tu-154M flying Chengdu-Wenzhou, was on approach when the crew extended flaps at 1,000 m; seconds later the nose dropped abruptly and the aircraft disintegrated in mid-air before crashing into high ground near Rui'an and exploding, killing all 61 aboard. The investigation found incorrect self-locking locknuts had been installed in the elevator system without maintenance crews noticing; the nuts worked loose in flight, leaving the elevator uncontrollable and disabling the pitch channel.
probable_cause: Incorrect self-locking locknuts installed in the elevator operating system went unnoticed by maintenance crews and spun off during the flight, leaving the elevator uncontrollable and disabling the pitch channel, causing the crash.

factors.evidence: Incorrect self-locking locknuts had been installed in the elevator operating system, which maintenance crews failed to notice
This disabled the aircraft's pitch channel, causing the crash
the aircraft's nose lowered abruptly, the aircraft disintegrated in mid-air and crashed into an area of high ground, and exploded

events.text: On 24 February 1999 the crew was preparing the aircraft for landing at Wenzhou Airport, and the flaps were extended at 1,000 m.
Seconds after flap extension, the aircraft's nose lowered abruptly, and it disintegrated in mid-air before crashing into high ground and exploding.
Investigators found incorrect self-locking locknuts in the elevator operating system, unnoticed by maintenance crews, had spun off during the flight, disabling the pitch channel.

title: LAPA 3142
summary: LAPA Flight 3142, a Boeing 737, crashed during takeoff from Buenos Aires on August 31, 1999. As the aircraft started its takeoff run, the take-off warning system sounded an alarm indicating incorrect configuration. The crew ignored the warning and continued the takeoff with flaps fully retracted. The aircraft overran the runway, breached the perimeter fence, crossed a road hitting a car, and collided with construction equipment before catching fire.
probable_cause: The crew failed to configure the aircraft correctly for takeoff, ignoring the take-off warning system alarm. The pilots did not verify flap position before proceeding with takeoff, and the aircraft was not airworthy according to regulatory requirements at the time of the accident.

factors.evidence: the aircraft was not correctly configured for takeoff with flaps not at the required takeoff position and instead fully retracted
the crew ignored the warning and continued, not realising that the flaps were not at the required takeoff position
it was mentioned that a pilot was allowed to fly without a license by the company
The jet overshot the runway, breaking through the airport's perimeter fence

events.text: Take-off warning system (TOWS) sounded an alarm indicating that the aircraft was not correctly configured for takeoff
The crew ignored the warning and continued
The crew continued takeoff roll as the aircraft was not realising the flaps were not at the required takeoff position
The jet overshot the runway, breaking through the airport's perimeter fence
Aircraft crossed a road, hitting an automobile in the process
Fuel spilling over the hot engines and gas leaking resulted in a fire that destroyed the aircraft

notes: Captain Weigel's license had expired at time of accident
Poor crew resource management and safety culture at LAPA
Captain allowed to fly without valid license per company policy
Crew had history of poor flying characteristics per records

title: EgyptAir 990

agencies.name: Egyptian Ministry of Civil Aviation's Civil Aviation Agency

summary: EgyptAir Flight 990, a Boeing 767 flying from Los Angeles to Cairo via New York, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean south of Nantucket on 31 October 1999, killing all 217 aboard. The NTSB concluded the aircraft departed normal cruise flight and dived into the ocean as a result of relief First Officer Gameel Al-Batouti's flight control inputs after he disengaged the autopilot and pushed the elevators nose-down while repeating 'I rely on God,' while Egypt's Civil Aviation Agency maintained the crash was caused by mechanical failure.
probable_cause: The NTSB's probable cause was the aircraft's departure from normal cruise flight and impact with the ocean as a result of relief First Officer Al-Batouti's flight control inputs, for which no specific reason could be determined; Egypt's ECAA independently concluded the crash was caused by mechanical failure.

factors.evidence: The NTSB found that the cause of the accident was the airplane's departure from normal cruise flight and subsequent impact with the Atlantic Ocean 'as a result of the relief first officer's flight control inputs'.
At 1:49:45 he disengaged the autopilot; the autopilot-disengagement warning was not heard on the CVR, indicating that the autopilot was disengaged manually.
Three seconds later, the throttles for both engines were reduced to idle, and both elevators were moved 3 degrees nose down.
The flight data recorder reflected that the elevators moved into a split condition, with the left elevator up and the right elevator down, during the abrupt maneuvers to recover from the dive.
The stress placed on the airframe caused structural integrity to fail at approximately 10,000 feet, with the left engine and other debris separating from the aircraft.

events.text: At 1:48, with the aircraft at its 33,000-foot cruising altitude, Captain El-Habashi left the cockpit for the lavatory, leaving relief First Officer Al-Batouti alone at the controls.
At 1:48:39 relief First Officer Al-Batouti began repeating 'I rely on God' in Egyptian Arabic.
At 1:49:45 the autopilot was disengaged manually, without triggering the disconnect warning on the cockpit voice recorder.
Three seconds after the autopilot disengaged, the throttles for both engines were reduced to idle and both elevators were moved three degrees nose down.

Radar data showed the aircraft entering a steep climb from 16,000 back to 25,000 feet between 1:50:38 and 1:51:15, with the elevators moving into a split condition of left elevator up and right elevator down.
At 1:51:15 the aircraft entered a second steep dive at around 20,000 feet per minute, and structural integrity failed at approximately 10,000 feet before impact with the ocean at 1:52 am.

notes: NTSB and Egypt's ECAA reached different conclusions about the cause; no motive for the relief first officer's actions was established.
